title: Thinking About Interior and Exterior Angles (Part 2 of 3): Deriving the Formula for the Sum of Interior Angles part-2-of-3-deriving-the-formula-for-the-sum-of-interior-angles/
author: Rowlandson, Paul
summary: Paul Rowlandson contrasts his early-career habit of jumping straight to the formula for the sum of interior angles with a slower, multi-method approach he now prefers, inspired by his 2017 visit to Tokyo with the IMPULS Project and Akihiko Takahashi's work on structured problem-solving in Japanese maths lessons. Rather than presenting the formula, he poses an open problem, split a pentagon into shapes with known angle sums and use that to deduce the pentagon's total, and lets the class produce genuinely different and sometimes contradictory answers, which become the object of structured comparison and debate rather than being corrected immediately. Through guided discussion, students discover for themselves that cutting from vertex to vertex avoids creating new, unwanted angles, and that any other cutting method can still be salvaged by explicitly subtracting the extra angles it introduces. He then shows how to synthesise several valid student-generated methods into a single general calculation by displaying them side by side, asking students to justify why visually different approaches are numerically equivalent, and finally replacing the varying numbers with algebra to arrive at the general formula, arguing that reaching the formula this way, as an endpoint of comparison rather than a given starting point, is what makes the generalisation meaningful rather than arbitrary.
points: Rowlandson deliberately withholds the formula, instead having students generate multiple methods, some flawed, and using the resulting disagreement between answers as the mechanism that drives mathematical reasoning.
His "cutting from vertex to vertex" resolution isn't asserted by the teacher; students derive it themselves by comparing which diagrams introduced new, unaccounted-for angles.

His synthesis step, displaying multiple valid methods side by side and asking students to justify their numerical equivalence, is presented as the pedagogically crucial step that's easy to skip in favour of just teaching the fastest method.
He credits Akihiko Takahashi's Japanese lesson-study model specifically for shifting his own view of mathematics away from a discipline where every problem-type has a single solution strategy.
quotes: There was nothing necessarily wrong with this method – after all, it is an efficient method, and the formula is usually the endpoint that I am aiming for. However, rushing to reach this endpoint as quickly as possible can sometimes bypass great opportunities for students to engage in some rich mathematical reasoning.
It seemed that most students thought the interior angles summed to either 540° or 900°. They agreed that both can’t be true and were asked to consider which answer seemed more likely to be correct.

The main conclusion from this episode was that the better method for splitting up a polygon (in order to calculate the sum of its interior angles) was by cutting from vertex to vertex. That way, it avoids creating any new vertices.
However, just because this way is better, it doesn’t mean that the other methods are wrong. They are just incomplete! Each one could be finished off by subtracting the new angles that were made.
By then replacing the variable numbers with algebra, we can generalise each calculation to produce a formula. Crucially: the same formula each time.
